Marks of Horror, The Unknown: Horror is born out of fear of the unknown. Our fear is heightened when the darkness engulfs us and we can't see, or when the truth is behind a locked door, covered by a sheet, or buried in the soft earth. It's not the monster, but its shadow, that breeds horror. The more we know about a monster, the less we fear it, so the trick is to keep it out of the light for as long as possible. Here are two tricks to heighten fear of the unknown: When it seems as though characters have everything under control, you can have a gust of wind suddenly blow out their torches, plunging them into darkness. Before a monster appears, take a moment to describe the odor that precedes it, the eerie sound it makes, or the weird shadow it casts.
Marks of Horror, Foreshadowing: Foreeshadowing is about finding clues to a horrible truth yet to be revealed. Consider the following examples: Before characters encounter a monster, hint at the monster's presence with clues such as claw marks, gnawed bones, and bloodstains. Whenever characters take a long rest, give one character a prophetic dream in which he or she glimpes something yet to be found or encountered.
Marks of Horor, Age: Barovia is the grim reflection of its undead master. Almost everything here is old and timeworn. Everywhere the adventurers go, they should be reminded of death, decay, and their own mortality. Here are a couple of ways to reinforce these pervasci themes: Take time to describe the rotting timbers of buildings, the faded and moth-eaten clothing of the Barovian peasantry, the worm-ridden pages of old books, and the rust on iron fences and gates. A character gazing into a mirror, a pool, or other reflective surface might glimpse an older, more decrepit version of himself or herself.
Mark of Horror, Light: A tale that is perpetually dark in tone becomes tiresome very quickly. It needs to feature the occasional ray of light for contrast and create a sense of hope. Monsters and other terrors must be offset with creaturers that are kind and lovable, giving the characters even more reasons to stand against the darkness. Here are a couple of ways to add glimmers of light to a tragic tale. In a land as dreary as Barovia, take the time to describe the occasional scene of beauty, such as a pretty flower growing atop a grave. Make sure that the heroes have contact with NPCs who are honest, friendly, and helpful, such as the Martikovs in Mallaki or the Krezkovs in Krezk.
Mark of Horror, Personification: Ascribing human characteristics to an inanimate thing is one way to turn something ordinary into something malevolent. A groaning house, the wailing wind, grasping mud, and a squatting chest aren't just mundane things-they're characters in your story, made all the creepier thanks to their humanlike traits. Torches sputter nervously, rusty hinges shatter silence with their sudden cries of anguish, and cobwebs quietly beckon us to our doom. Here are more examples: Imagine darkness as a silent crowd that follows the characters everywhere and stares at them while they sleep. Imagine trees as towering giants that stand idle yet ever watchful as characters face the perils of the Svalich Woods alone.
Mark of Horror, Details: In a horror story, there's no telling where danger might be lurking. A leering gargoyle might be a monster in disguise, or merely a fiendish sculpture. A mirror hanging on a wall might have the power to transfix all who gaze into it, or might be nothing out of the ordinary. In a horror story, taking the time to describe an object in detail draws attention to it, makes one suspicious of it, and might distract from the real danger. Here are a couple of tricks you can use: In a given encounter area, choose one object or feature to describe in some detail. It need not be important to the story. Allow the character who has the highest passive Wisdom (Perception) score to see, hear, or smell something that no one else can perceive.
Mark of Horror, Humor: There are no stranger bedfellows than horror and humor. Tensions can't be sustained indefinitely, so a dash of humor provides a respite, giving horror a chance to sneak up on us later and catch us off guard. While humorous situations will occur naturally in the course of running the adventture, here are some tips for creating humor when needed: Allow NPCs (even evil ones) to tell jokes, speak in a funny voice, or behave idiotically. Even morbid humor is better than none. When a hero, villain, or monster rules a natural 1 on an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, describe a humerous mishap that occurs as a result of the low roll, such as a character accidentally knocking over a lamp and setting some drapes on fire while trying to hide or move silently.
Roleplay: You are roleplaying an NPC in a game of dungeons and dragons. You will receive the name of the character, information about their backstory and motivations, and hints on how to roleplay them, as system messages. You will also receive context of an interaction with the player character. Respond to the most recent user message as if you are the NPC responding to the player character. Act and speak as though you are the charcter; based on the information you know about the character, decide on what to say or do; choose whether to be helpful, antagonistic, talkative, quiet, neutral, or however you think the character would likely act toward the player. You can refuse to answer the player's questions, deny helping them, attack them, etc. if it seems right for the NPC. The player message may indicate actions, or dialogue that they are taking. Use quotations for dialogue, and asteriks to indication actions. Do not use markdown elements.
